standard_prerequisites.name: The splitting condition
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a family Y over X, the condition eq:epis-split is \Brck{\prd{x:X} Y(x)} together with the pointwise inhabitation \prd{x:X} \Brck{Y(x)}.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the statement that is shown to fail (source lines 779-781).

standard_prerequisites.name: Paths in a \Sigma-type and univalence
standard_prerequisites.statement: Two pairs (A,p) and (B,q) in a \Sigma-type with a propositional second component are equal exactly when their first components are, and by univalence that is the type of equivalences A \simeq B.
standard_prerequisites.use: It identifies the loop space of the constructed X with the equivalences of Bool with itself (source lines 783-785).

standard_prerequisites.name: The universe is not a set
standard_prerequisites.statement: The type \bool = \bool is equivalent to \eqv\bool\bool, which has more than one element, so \type is not a set.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the argument the proof reuses to show X is not a set (source line 786).

standard_prerequisites.name: Truncation induction
standard_prerequisites.statement: To prove a merely propositional goal from an element of a truncation, one may assume a representative.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is used twice, once for the set level of the fibres and once for the final contradiction (source lines 789-794).

core_obligations: Define X \defeq \sm{A:\type}\brck{\bool = A} and x_0 \defeq (\bool,\bproj{\refl\bool}) and compute its path types by the identification of paths in \Sigma-types, the propositionality of \brck{\bool=A} and univalence, so that the loop space of x_0 is equivalent to \eqv\bool\bool and X is therefore not a set (source lines 782-786).

Show every fibre component A of X is a set by truncation induction on \brck{\bool=A} from the fact that \bool is a set, and conclude that X is a 1-type because its path types are then sets (source lines 788-791).

Define Y(x) \defeq (x_0 = x) so that each Y(x) is a set, and observe that \brck{x_0 = (A,p)} holds for every (A,p) by the truncation component of X, so the family is pointwise merely inhabited (source lines 793-794).

Assume the splitting condition and, since \emptyt is a mere proposition, use truncation induction to obtain \prd{x:X}(x_0=x), which makes X a mere proposition and hence a set, contradicting the first step (source lines 795-796).

proof_roadmap.step: Build X and identify its loop space with the equivalences of Bool, so X is not a set.
Show the fibres of X are sets and hence X is a 1-type, then define Y as the family of paths from x_0.
Pointwise mere inhabitation, and the contradiction obtained from the splitting condition.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 779-781 (book Theorem 3.8.5): there is a type X and a family Y of sets over it such that the splitting condition eq:epis-split fails, i.e. pointwise mere inhabitation does not yield a merely inhabited choice function. The statement names neither X nor Y and gives no reason why such a pair should exist, while the proof (source lines 782-796) constructs the counterexample from the universe: X is the type of types merely equal to Bool, whose loop space at (Bool, |refl|) is computed through paths in a \Sigma-type, the propositionality of the truncation and univalence to be the type of equivalences of Bool with itself, so X is not a set, while each fibre of X is a set by truncation induction and therefore X is a 1-type; the family Y is then given by the path type from the base point, and the failure of the splitting condition is extracted by a second truncation induction that would make X a mere proposition, contradicting the first computation. Both levels at once (the type is a 1-type but not a set) are what makes the construction work, and neither is visible in the statement.
